# Practice — Building an Architecture Reasoning Agent (Kiro IDE edition)

Testing PR workflow. test

In this practice you will build agents from scratch: an engineering team
lead chatbot, an architecture reasoning orchestrator, and an RFC writer
sub-agent. The tools and data are provided — your job is to write the
agent instructions.

Everything runs inside **Kiro IDE**. You open the repository **once** at
its root and switch between agents using the **agent picker** — there is
no `cd` into sub-folders and no terminal launch command.

The target codebase is the **Conduit RealWorld** app
(`conduit-realworld-example-app/`), a Medium-clone with a
Node.js/Express backend, Sequelize + PostgreSQL, and a React/Vite
frontend.

Three team lead personas are provided as ready-to-use agents — each
requests a different feature. Pick one to start:

| Persona | Agent (in picker) | Feature requested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Alex Chen** | `alex-chen` | Real-time collaborative article editing |
| **Marcus Webb** | `marcus-webb` | AI-powered personalized article feed |
| **Priya Sharma** | `priya-sharma` | Premium subscription + revenue share |

---

## Repository layout

```text
agent-arch-reasoning-practice/
├── conduit-realworld-example-app/
│   ├── backend/                    ← Express + Sequelize + PostgreSQL
│   └── frontend/                   ← React + Vite SPA
│
├── data/
│   ├── context/company.md          ← business context, pain points
│   ├── adrs/
│   │   ├── ADR-001-database.md
│   │   ├── ADR-002-api-design.md
│   │   └── ADR-003-deployment.md
│   └── diagrams/
│       └── current-architecture.mmd
│
├── .kiro/
│   ├── agents/
│   │   ├── alex-chen.md
│   │   ├── marcus-webb.md
│   │   ├── priya-sharma.md
│   │   └── architect_template.template.md
│   ├── skills/
│   │   └── adr-tools/
│   │       ├── SKILL.md
│   │       └── scripts/
│   │           ├── list_adrs.py
│   │           ├── read_adr.py
│   │           ├── write_adr.py
│   │           └── save_diagram.py
│   └── settings/
│       └── mcp.json
│
├── output/
│   ├── adrs/
│   └── diagrams/
│
└── README.md
```

The three persona agents are **complete and ready to use** — you select
them in the picker, you do not build them. The only agent you build is
the **architect**, from the template.

---

## Step 0 — Setup

Open the repository root in Kiro IDE. Open the agent picker and confirm
it lists `alex-chen`, `marcus-webb`, and `priya-sharma`. (If it does
not, reopen the workspace — agents register at session start.)

Verify the skill scripts work from a terminal:

```bash
python3 .kiro/skills/adr-tools/scripts/list_adrs.py
python3 .kiro/skills/adr-tools/scripts/read_adr.py ADR-001
```

> If `python3` is not found, use `python` instead (or `py` on Windows).
> Confirm with `python3 --version` / `python --version` that it reports
> **Python 3.x**.

Read `data/context/company.md` to understand the scenario, then browse
`conduit-realworld-example-app/backend/` to see the actual code the
agent will reason about.

---

## Step 1 — Talk to a Team Lead

Pick one persona (or try all three for extra practice). Select its agent
in the picker — e.g. `alex-chen` — and start a conversation. The
persona loads immediately; it does not introduce itself as Kiro.

**Good opening questions by persona:**

- Alex: *"What exactly should two writers be able to do at the same
  time?"*
- Marcus: *"What data do you have today that a recommendation engine
  could use?"*
- Priya: *"What happens if we charge a reader and the server crashes
  before we record it?"*

The team lead answers in product/delivery language and pushes back when
proposals sound complex or slow to ship. Note down the requirements you
gather — you will feed them to the architect in Step 3.

---

## Step 2 — Read and analyse the existing ADRs

Before building the agent, spend 10 minutes reading the three ADRs in
`data/adrs/` manually (just open them in the editor — no agent at this
stage).

- What was decided and when?
- Which ADR explicitly flags that real-time features need a different
  transport layer?
- What does ADR-003 warn about for multi-process WebSocket deployments?

This shapes the requirements section of your agent.

---

## Step 3 — Build the Architecture Reasoning Agent

This is the main agent. It reads ADRs, identifies gaps, proposes
options, generates diagrams, and writes new ADRs.

The template is `.kiro/agents/architect_template.template.md`. You do
**not** fill it in by hand — you ask Kiro to generate the filled-in
config for you, then review and tune it. Save the result as
`.kiro/agents/architect.md` and set its header `name:` to `architect`
— that is what makes it appear in the picker as **architect**.

> **Why the template's `name:` is a placeholder.** Kiro indexes the
> `name:` field, so the picker would list any agent file that declares a
> real name — even the half-filled `*.template.md` skeleton. To keep
> the unfinished skeleton out of the picker, the template ships with an
> inert `name:` (`architect-TEMPLATE-rename-me`). When you save your
> completed copy as `architect.md`, change `name:` to `architect`.

Required sections the generated config must fill in:

| Section | What it must contain |
| --- | --- |
| **Your role** | One-sentence identity |
| **Purpose** | Full scope: what the agent reads, analyses, produces |
| **Trigger** | Exact phrases that start the workflow |
| **Skills** | Load `adr-tools` via the `resources` field |
| **Sub-agents** | The three team leads, invokable to resolve ambiguity |
| **Workflow** | Ordered steps (see hints in template) |
| **Output format** | Gap analysis table + options with costs/risks/timelines |
| **Guardrails** | ADR write gate and diagram gate |
| **Failure handling** | What to do when each tool or sub-agent fails |

### Required guardrails

The generated `architect.md` **must** include both of these rules:

> `write_adr` must **not** be called unless the user's message contains
> **"write adr"**, **"save adr"**, or **"publish"**.
>
> `save_diagram` must **not** be called before the user has selected a
> specific option.

Once `architect.md` exists, select **architect** in the picker (reopen
it if needed) and send: `analyse the architecture`

Confirm it:

- Reads `company.md` and all 3 ADRs
- Identifies at least 3 architectural gaps related to the feature
- Proposes 2–3 options with cost estimates and timelines
- **Waits** — does not call `write_adr` or `save_diagram` yet

Then drive it through the full flow:

- Select an option → a diagram is saved to `output/diagrams/`
- Say `write adr` → an ADR is saved to `output/adrs/`

---

## Step 4 — Add an RFC writer sub-agent

After the agent writes an ADR, it should produce a complete RFC that
combines everything: requirements, architecture, ADRs, diagram, and
migration plan. Rather than make the architect do this itself, you hand
off to a second, focused agent — an RFC writer.

You build the RFC writer the same way as the architect: ask Kiro to
generate the agent config from a brief, then wire the architect to hand
off to it once the ADR is written. The RFC writer receives, in its
prompt from the architect:

- Full company context
- All ADR content (existing + new)
- The selected architecture option with its rationale
- The diagram path in `output/diagrams/`
- The requirements summary from the team-lead interview

Re-run the full workflow and verify an RFC is written to `output/`.
Read it as the team lead would: could someone approve or reject the
decision from this document alone, without having watched the
conversation?

---

## Step 5 — Live diagrams with the Mermaid MCP server

The architecture agent can render and live-preview Mermaid diagrams in
your browser using the **`claude-mermaid`** MCP server (an npm package
— despite the name it works with any MCP client, not just Claude). This
is optional but recommended — without it the agent still writes
`.mmd`/`.svg` files via the `save_diagram` skill, but you don't get
the live browser preview.

### Prerequisite (install before the workshop)

The server pulls in Puppeteer + Chromium (a few hundred MB on first run)
and **requires Node ≥ 22.12**. Install it ahead of time on a supported
Node so it does not download live during the session:

**macOS / Linux (nvm):**

```bash
nvm install 22 && nvm use 22
npm install -g claude-mermaid

# verify (prints "Claude Mermaid MCP Server running on stdio", then Ctrl-C)
claude-mermaid
```

**Windows:** `nvm install` is a Mac/Linux tool. Use one of:

- Download the **Node 22 LTS** installer from
  [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org) and run it, or
- Install [nvm-windows](https://github.com/coreybutler/nvm-windows)
  and run `nvm install 22` then `nvm use 22`.

Then install and verify the server the same way (PowerShell or Command
Prompt):

```powershell
npm install -g claude-mermaid

# verify (prints "Claude Mermaid MCP Server running on stdio", then Ctrl-C)
claude-mermaid
```

Confirm your Node version with `node --version` (must be ≥ 22.12).

### Configuration

The repo ships `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` with the server already
declared:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mermaid": {
      "command": "claude-mermaid",
      "args": [],
      "disabled": false,
      "autoApprove": ["mermaid_preview", "mermaid_save"]
    }
  }
}
```

Kiro IDE reloads MCP config on save — no restart needed. Open the MCP
panel (`/mcp`) and confirm **mermaid** shows as connected with its
**2 tools** (`mermaid_preview`, `mermaid_save`). The `autoApprove`
entry means you are not prompted to allow those tool calls during the
exercise.

> If the panel shows "connecting" forever or "command not found", the
> binary is not on your `PATH`. Find it with `which claude-mermaid`
> (macOS/Linux) or `where claude-mermaid` (Windows) and put that
> absolute path in `command`.

### Verify it works

With the **architect** selected, after you have picked an option, ask
it to draw the target architecture and open a live preview. A browser
tab opens at `http://localhost:3737` and auto-refreshes as the diagram
is refined.

**Offline fallback:** if the MCP server is unavailable, have the agent
output raw Mermaid and paste it into [mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live).

---

## Submission checklist

- [ ] A team lead persona was used from the picker
- [ ] Team lead chatbot responds in delivery/product language
- [ ] `.kiro/agents/architect.md` exists — no `[TODO]` tokens remain
- [ ] ADR write gate present in `architect.md`
- [ ] Diagram gate present in `architect.md`
- [ ] Agent reads all 3 ADRs before proposing options
- [ ] Agent presents 2–3 options and **waits** before writing anything
- [ ] `output/diagrams/` contains a generated diagram
- [ ] `output/adrs/` contains a generated ADR
- [ ] An RFC writer agent was built and the architect hands off to it
- [ ] An RFC exists in `output/` after a full workflow run

---

## Tips

- Read `data/context/company.md` carefully — your agent's gap analysis
  should map directly to the pain points described there, especially the
  single-VPS constraint that affects WebSocket scaling.
- Browse `conduit-realworld-example-app/backend/` — the agent should
  reason about what the real code actually does, not just the company
  doc.
- The write gate is the most important guardrail. Test that the agent
  does **not** call `write_adr` when you say "looks good" or
  "I approve".
- If the agent skips a step, add more explicit ordering language to the
  workflow section — but add rules only against a flaw you actually
  observe, not pre-emptively.

# Hardcoded API key introduced in payment_service.py

This change adds a single new file, `payment_service.py`, whose only content is a bare string assignment `api_key = "sk-12345..."`. The file has no imports, no functions, no classes, and no consumers — it exists solely to store a credential as a Python module-level variable. The API key is committed in plaintext to version history, where it will persist even after future removal.

**Watch for:** The secret is now in git history permanently (**confirmed**). The key appears to be a real or real-formatted credential and must be rotated immediately if it was ever valid. There are no design elements here worth salvaging; the approach itself is the problem.

**Verdict**: NEEDS_CHANGES

---

## High-level view

A single-line file that stores a secret as a hardcoded Python variable is not a payment service — it is a credential exposure. Beyond the security dimension, the file introduces no callable interface, no integration with any payment provider, and no mechanism to vary the key across environments. Even if the secret concern were resolved, the file represents an empty placeholder with no functional content. The commit description ("Add API key for payment service") accurately describes what was done, which makes the design intent, not just an implementation slip, the concern here.

---

<details>
<summary>Issues (4)</summary>

1. **Hardcoded secret in version control** — `api_key = "sk-12345..."` is committed to git history. Even if the line is deleted in a follow-up commit, the value remains accessible via `git log`. Rotate the key immediately if it has ever been active, then remove the value from history (using `git filter-repo` or equivalent) and store the secret in an environment variable or secrets manager.

2. **No secrets management pattern** — The correct approach is `api_key = os.environ["PAYMENT_API_KEY"]`, failing fast at startup if the variable is absent. This keeps the key out of source control entirely and makes environment-specific configuration explicit.

3. **No callable surface** — The file is a module with one variable and nothing else. There are no functions, no classes, no integration with a payment provider SDK. Any code that imports this will access the credential directly, scattering the secret reference across the codebase rather than encapsulating it.

4. **No tests** — There are no tests at all in this diff. A payment service integration, even a stub, warrants at minimum a test that the key is loaded from the environment and that an absent key raises a clear startup error.

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

## Credential exposure via plaintext assignment

The key is assigned as a string literal at module scope: `api_key = "sk-12345..."`. Every language runtime that imports this module will have the value in memory, and every git client that has cloned the repository since this commit has the value on disk. The `sk-` prefix pattern is associated with several payment and AI provider key formats, suggesting this is a real or real-formatted secret rather than a placeholder.

Mitigation has two independent steps. First, rotate the key — assume it is compromised from the moment it landed in a commit. Second, remove it from history. Deleting the file or the line in a future commit does not remove the value from `git log`; that requires a history rewrite. Tools like `git filter-repo` or the GitHub secret scanning alert workflow can help here, but the key rotation must happen regardless of whether history is cleaned.

## Missing environment-based configuration

```python
import os

api_key = os.environ["PAYMENT_API_KEY"]
```

Reading from the environment at startup fails loudly on misconfiguration — a missing variable raises `KeyError` before any payment call is attempted. `os.environ.get("PAYMENT_API_KEY")` with an explicit `None` check at the call site is the right pattern when the key is optional in some environments, but a payment service has no meaningful code path without it, so the strict form is appropriate here.

## No functional payment service structure

The file provides no abstraction over the payment provider. A minimal useful module would wrap the key in a client object, expose functions for charge, refund, and status operations, and centralise the credential reference so callers never touch the key directly. As written, any file that does `from payment_service import api_key` will hold the credential directly, making it harder to audit usage or rotate the key in a single place.

## Test coverage

No tests accompany this change. The absence is notable for a payment path: at minimum, a test that the module raises a clear error when `PAYMENT_API_KEY` is unset, and a smoke test that the client can be instantiated against a mock provider, would catch environment misconfiguration before it reaches production.

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>Files changed</summary>

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `payment_service.py` | New file — single-line module that assigns a hardcoded API key string to a module-level variable |

</details>

</content>

# Hardcoded API key introduced in payment_service.py

This change adds a single new file, `payment_service.py`, whose only content is a bare string assignment `api_key = "sk-12345..."`. The file has no imports, no functions, no classes, and no consumers — it exists solely to store a credential as a Python module-level variable. A single-line file that stores a secret as a hardcoded Python variable is not a payment service — it is a credential exposure. Beyond the security dimension, the file introduces no callable interface, no integration with any payment provider, and no mechanism to vary the key across environments. Even if the secret concern were resolved, the file represents an empty placeholder with no functional content. The commit description ("Add API key for payment service") accurately describes what was done, which makes the design intent, not just an implementation slip, the concern here.

<summary>Issues (4)</summary>

3. **No callable surface** — The file is a module with one variable and nothing else. There are no functions, no classes, no integration with a payment provider SDK. 4. **No tests** — There are no tests at all in this diff. A payment service integration, even a stub, warrants at minimum a test that the key is loaded from the environment and that an absent key raises a clear startup error.

</details>

---

<summary>Details</summary>

## Credential exposure via plaintext assignment

The key is assigned as a string literal at module scope: `api_key = "sk-12345..."`. Deleting the file or the line in a future commit does not remove the value from `git log`; that requires a history rewrite. ```python

# Hardcoded API key introduced in payment_service.py

This change adds a single new file, `payment_service.py`, whose only content is a bare string assignment `api_key = "sk-12345..."`. The file has no imports, no functions, no classes, and no consumers — it exists solely to store a credential as a Python module-level variable. The API key is committed in plaintext to version history, where it will persist even after future removal.

**Watch for:** The secret is now in git history permanently (**confirmed**). The key appears to be a real or real-formatted credential and must be rotated immediately if it was ever valid. There are no design elements here worth salvaging; the approach itself is the problem.

**Verdict**: NEEDS_CHANGES

---

## High-level view

A single-line file that stores a secret as a hardcoded Python variable is not a payment service — it is a credential exposure. Beyond the security dimension, the file introduces no callable interface, no integration with any payment provider, and no mechanism to vary the key across environments. Even if the secret concern were resolved, the file represents an empty placeholder with no functional content. The commit description ("Add API key for payment service") accurately describes what was done, which makes the design intent, not just an implementation slip, the concern here.

---

<details>
<summary>Issues (4)</summary>

1. **Hardcoded secret in version control** — `api_key = "sk-12345..."` is committed to git history. Even if the line is deleted in a follow-up commit, the value remains accessible via `git log`. Rotate the key immediately if it has ever been active, then remove the value from history (using `git filter-repo` or equivalent) and store the secret in an environment variable or secrets manager.

2. **No secrets management pattern** — The correct approach is `api_key = os.environ["PAYMENT_API_KEY"]`, failing fast at startup if the variable is absent. This keeps the key out of source control entirely and makes environment-specific configuration explicit.

3. **No callable surface** — The file is a module with one variable and nothing else. There are no functions, no classes, no integration with a payment provider SDK. Any code that imports this will access the credential directly, scattering the secret reference across the codebase rather than encapsulating it.

4. **No tests** — There are no tests at all in this diff. A payment service integration, even a stub, warrants at minimum a test that the key is loaded from the environment and that an absent key raises a clear startup error.

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

## Credential exposure via plaintext assignment

The key is assigned as a string literal at module scope: `api_key = "sk-12345..."`. Every language runtime that imports this module will have the value in memory, and every git client that has cloned the repository since this commit has the value on disk. The `sk-` prefix pattern is associated with several payment and AI provider key formats, suggesting this is a real or real-formatted secret rather than a placeholder.

Mitigation has two independent steps. First, rotate the key — assume it is compromised from the moment it landed in a commit. Second, remove it from history. Deleting the file or the line in a future commit does not remove the value from `git log`; that requires a history rewrite. Tools like `git filter-repo` or the GitHub secret scanning alert workflow can help here, but the key rotation must happen regardless of whether history is cleaned.

```python

api_key = os.environ["PAYMENT_API_KEY"]
```

Reading from the environment at startup fails loudly on misconfiguration — a missing variable raises `KeyError` before any payment call is attempted. `os.environ.get("PAYMENT_API_KEY")` with an explicit `None` check at the call site is the right pattern when the key is optional in some environments, but a payment service has no meaningful code path without it, so the strict form is appropriate here.

As written, any file that does `from payment_service import api_key` will hold the credential directly, making it harder to audit usage or rotate the key in a single place.

## Test coverage

No tests accompany this change. The absence is notable for a payment path: at minimum, a test that the module raises a clear error when `PAYMENT_API_KEY` is unset, and a smoke test that the client can be instantiated against a mock provider, would catch environment misconfiguration before it reaches production.

</details>

A single-line file that stores a secret as a hardcoded Python variable is not a payment service — it is a credential exposure. Beyond the security dimension, the file introduces no callable interface, no integration with any payment provider, and no mechanism to vary the key across environments. Even if the secret concern were resolved, the file represents an empty placeholder with no functional content. A single-line file that stores a secret as a hardcoded Python variable is not
a payment service — it is a credential exposure. Beyond the security dimension,
the file introduces no callable interface, no integration with any payment
provider, and no mechanism to vary the key across environments. Even if the
secret concern were resolved, the file represents an empty placeholder with no
functional content. The commit description ("Add API key for payment service")
accurately describes what was done, which makes the design intent, not just an
implementation slip, the concern here.

---

## Details

### Credential exposure via plaintext assignment

The key is assigned as a string literal at module scope:
`api_key = "sk-12345..."`. Every language runtime that imports this module will
have the value in memory, and every git client that has cloned the repository
since this commit has the value on disk. The `sk-` prefix pattern is associated
with several payment and AI provider key formats, suggesting this is a real or
real-formatted secret rather than a placeholder.

Mitigation has two independent steps. First, rotate the key — assume it is
compromised from the moment it landed in a commit. Second, remove it from
history. Deleting the file or the line in a future commit does not remove the
value from `git log`; that requires a history rewrite. Tools like
`git filter-repo` or the GitHub secret scanning alert workflow can help here,
but the key rotation must happen regardless of whether history is cleaned.

### Missing environment-based configuration

```python
import os

api_key = os.environ["PAYMENT_API_KEY"]
```

Reading from the environment at startup fails loudly on misconfiguration — a
missing variable raises `KeyError` before any payment call is attempted.
`os.environ.get("PAYMENT_API_KEY")` with an explicit `None` check at the call
site is the right pattern when the key is optional in some environments, but a
payment service has no meaningful code path without it, so the strict form is
appropriate here.

### No functional payment service structure

The file provides no abstraction over the payment provider. A minimal useful
module would wrap the key in a client object, expose functions for charge,
refund, and status operations, and centralise the credential reference so
callers never touch the key directly. As written, any file that does
`from payment_service import api_key` will hold the credential directly, making
it harder to audit usage or rotate the key in a single place.

### Test coverage

No tests accompany this change. The absence is notable for a payment path: at
minimum, a test that the module raises a clear error when `PAYMENT_API_KEY` is
unset, and a smoke test that the client can be instantiated against a mock
provider, would catch environment misconfiguration before it reaches production.
